text:
Spreads - the thread that binds products

It's easy to follow crude prices via Brent or WTI or even diesel via ICE GO. But the clearer trends are usually in spreads and they tell a lot more about what's happening than flatprice.

In the refinery, product yields are not fixed. There is always some optimization you can do to increase the yield of jet vs diesel, diesel vs fuel oil, diesel vs mogas, etc etc because oil product specifications have some leeway, unlike say petrochemical products which are more stringent in nature.

The spread that is easiest to understand in the kero regrade, i.e. jet price minus diesel price. If it's positive, then jet is more distressed than diesel, which happened at the very start of the US-Iran war back in March. Now the regrade is negative because the tightness is in diesel, not jet.

What I am monitoring closely is the diesel - gasoline spreads. Sg 10 - Sing 92 hit a high of $60/bbl in mid Sep. But we all still need refineries to make gasoline, so that spread cannot remain this high for too long.  Diesel basically then pulled mogas prices up while diesel itself fell a little. (I still can't figure out why the crack went south, but the Sg 10 - Sing 92 spread makes sense).

There's also the FOGO to watch, which is Sing 380 - Sg 10. That same bounce happened in mid September after hitting a very low point. We still need marine fuel alright because it can't just be a diesel story.

So watch those inter product spreads - they are the threads that bind.

Saudi E/W pipeline outage update
13 Sep 26 - 15:00 CEST

1⃣ According to the Ministry of Energy, the Saudi East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions was subjected to multiple attacks on Thursday 10 September. The pipeline has been shutdown as a precautionary measure. This pipeline typically carries Arab Light and Arab Heavy crude, both to domestic refineries and to the export markets.

2⃣ Duration of the outage is unknown. The attacks apparently came from Iraq, and not directly related to the Houthis that had seized the port city of Mocha on Thursday.

3⃣ If the pipelines flows are restored within a short time, there should have enough buffer within the system to keep the domestic refineries running. However exports of crude via the Red Sea will be met with some difficulty after drawing down from tank inventories at Yanbu.

4⃣ Additionally production shut-ins are likely if the crude stocks hits tank top on the Eastern side of Saudi. We anticipate dirty freight availability to be the key constraint in managing the evacuation option ex Ras Tanura. This will support TD3c markets further.

5⃣ European refiners (particularly in the Med) that have been relying on Saudi crude ex Sidi Kerir will also face temporary prompt shortages. This will mirror how Asian refineries reacted at the onset of the SoH closure, whereby reducing runrates is the likely outcome while waiting for viable crude replacements to arrive.

6⃣ Eastern refiners are not fully spared from this scenario as well since Korea and Japan have been seen chartering cargoes ex-Sidi Kerir but at least they may still benefit from getting crude ex Gulf of Oman in a shorter time if Saudi is able to offer this option.

7⃣ 400 kbd YASREF refinery, 400 kbd SAMREF and 245 kbd Yanbu refinery exports products, mainly distillates. If the pipeline outage exceeds the time the refineries have on available crude buffers, then the refineries may be forced to shutdown later due to crude unavailability. This is the likely worst case scenario which will only happen if the pipeline is out for an extended period of time.

8⃣ This means the diesel tightness we have seen in Europe will become further exacerbated with some Med refineries turning down on intake in the prompt while reevaluating crude replacement options, and potentially facing the worst-case scenario of the Saudi refineries themselves not exporting products.

9⃣ Thus we are likely going to see higher flatprice, Brent-Dubai EFS, DFL, prompt crude timespreads, crude FOB diffs, diesel timespreads and even stronger cracks when we start the week, until further clarity is found. This is of course subject to any new headlines of peace deals that can quickly temper the excitement.

🔟 Jet and mogas cracks will likely be pulled up by the diesel strength. Dirty freight could also move up with more inefficient freight routings anticipated.

An extended outage could also see IEA coming in with further SPR release to calm the markets, but that buffer is getting thinner.

We analyzed how @claudeai’s Opus 5.5 writes compared with Opus 5 across high-reasoning Text Arena outputs.

10 of 12 writing measures moved in a better direction.

Opus 5.5 should be easier to read:
- Long content words fall from 41.7% to 38.6%, the lowest share of any Claude model we analyzed.
- Sentences are 17% shorter on average, dropping from 12.14 to 10.03 words.

The tradeoff is length. Answers get 6% wordier, rising from 453 to 481 words on average, making Opus 5.5 give the longest answers across the Opus family. 

It also sounds less recognizably AI on two familiar tells:
- 95% fewer em dashes
- 73% fewer semicolons

But a new giveaway may be emerging. Hedges and caveats such as “perhaps” and “arguably” rise 97%, from 0.39 to 0.77 per 1,000 words, the highest rate of any Claude model we analyzed.

What do you think: does Opus 5.5 read more naturally?

Two Reuters reports, same Beijing Swing complications story.

Domestic Chinese fuel prices are still much lower than they should be, held lower by domestic price caps.

That causes all kinds of unfortunate distortions and means Beijing can't further ease export restrictions without Chinese refiners effectively shipping commercial stocks abroad where they're worth of heck of a lot more.

But this reality is also keeping Chinese refining runs much lower than they should be, because their realized margins are crap, when all other refiners are running flat out because global margins are the best they've ever been.

Balance of evidence indicates that Beijing is supplementing this domestic fuel imbalance with [unobservable/strategic] stocks, which means this can't go on forever.

Either Hormuz has to *really* open soon or Chinese pump prices are going to need to rise—status quo remains fundamentally unsustainable.

Thinking through this further, whether a diesel export ban comes with a hard sunset date is a massive pivot point. If we're talking 2-3 month temporary freeze like the rumor mill suggests, the policy looks way more destructive than constructive.

For starters, refiners don't have much room to just pivot yields into jet fuel. US refiners have already been running near max jet yield, so even if the regrade swings wildly, the immediate swing capacity is pretty capped.

Then you have term contracts. A huge chunk of US diesel exports is locked into long term contracts (someone check me on the exact %). Would a sudden export ban even trigger Force Majeure?

Guaranteed there are contracts where FM doesn't hold water. In that case, US refiners are on the hook to source replacement barrels at blown-out global benchmark premiums to meet delivery commitments abroad.

Run cuts will happen, but a brief 2–3 month ban won't crush utilization rates overnight. That means US refiners get squeezed from both ends, still pulling in expensive crude feedstocks(crude imports) while eating cratered margins on trapped domestic outlight price.

They could easily torch well north of $5B on this lmao. It's completely unsustainable and sets up massive structural scars down the line. It would bleed back into upstream US crude production too, which completely backfires on long term price mgmt.

If the US were a completely closed autarky with zero crude imports, maybe this policy moves the needle. But that’s not the tape we live in. All it does is briefly artificially pin domestic prices at the expense of inviting a wave of medium term blowbacks.

Awful policy all around. Still doubt they pull the trigger on a ban, but they just flat-out shouldn't.

There is absolutely no observational evidence to support this. And it isn’t supported by physics either.

Extratropical cyclones (which is what nor’easters are) are baroclinic storms. That means their energy is derived from available potential energy stored in large-scale temperature gradients: cold continental air versus warmer maritime air. The stronger the latitudinal (equator-to-pole) temperature difference, the higher the vertical wind shear, and the faster a cyclone can grow by converting that stored energy into kinetic.

The first-order thermodynamic effect of polar amplification (a byproduct of global warming) is to reduce that gradient and starve baroclinic storms of their primary energy source.

BCOM. The Bloomberg Commodity Index is heading for its first, albeit modest, weekly loss in four weeks, down 0.8% and trimming its year-to-date gain to 36%. A stronger dollar and surging bond yields weighed on sentiment across markets, particularly precious metals, while geopolitical risks ebbed and flowed, leaving the energy sector lower overall. Diesel, EU gas and silver are the three biggest weekly losers, while gains are led by US natural gas, cocoa and sugar.

Oil. Brent trades near unchanged on the week at around USD 105.4, having moved within a range of more than USD 10 amid a steady flow of mixed supply and geopolitical developments from the Middle East. The latest focus is on US and Iranian negotiators exploring a phased deal that could see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz if certain conditions are met. Meanwhile, the prospect of a Trump-backed US diesel export ban sent fuel prices sharply higher earlier in the week before they eased as the industry warned that any short-term reduction in domestic prices could prove fleeting - and potentially be followed by higher costs - as rising US fuel inventories prompt producers and refiners to cut output.

Metals. Gold is down around 3% and silver 5% on the week as investment metals faced a bond-market stress test, with surging Treasury yields supporting a stronger dollar and raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets. Despite these macro headwinds, bullion has remained relatively rangebound over the past month, with traders monitoring support around USD 4,235 and resistance currently near USD 4,400.

Natural gas. Despite a midweek surge, Europe's TTF benchmark is heading for a weekly loss of around 6.5%, trading near EUR 73/MWh (USD 24.30/MMBtu), amid signs that more LNG cargoes have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz. In contrast, the US Henry Hub contract has surged almost 9% after a major pipeline disruption helped trigger a short squeeze as traders reduced sizeable bearish positions. From a low of USD 2.82/MMBBtu on Tuesday, the front-month contract briefly touched USD 3.30 on Thursday before easing back towards USD 3.20.

A midweek surge of more than 16% in the US Henry Hub #natgas contract briefly lifted the front-month future above USD 3.30/MMBtu, an 11-week high, after trading as low as USD 2.82 on Tuesday. The rally was triggered by a major pipeline disruption in Appalachia affecting flows equivalent to around 1.6% of total US gas supply, compounding an already tighter production backdrop as producers have been shutting in output for several weeks ahead of the seasonally weak autumn shoulder period. Overall, the front-month contract is heading for a weekly gain of more than 9%, its best week since May.

The tightening supply picture has been reinforced by storage data. The EIA reported a smaller-than-normal inventory build for a sixth consecutive week, further eroding the storage cushion and leaving stocks just 2.9% above the five-year average. With speculative positioning heavily tilted towards the short side ahead of the disruption, the combination of lower production, constrained pipeline flows and a shrinking storage surplus helped trigger a sharp short-covering rally.
